message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated this number to be on the order of

\[
N \approx 10^{43}
\]

This figure is often called the **Shannon number**.  It represents a lower bound on the true count of legal positions; more recent computational studies suggest the actual number may be closer to \(10^{46}\), but the exact value is still unknown because enumerating every possible position is computationally infeasible.

So, in short, there are roughly **10 to the 43rd power** possible arrangements (legal positions) in chess.
